item.content:encoded:
"Zero tolerance against terrorism": HM Amit Shah hails extension of ban on Zakir Naik led IRF The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) on Friday extended the ban on the Islamic Research Foundation (IRF), led by fugitive preacher Dr Zakir Naik, declaring the organisation an unlawful association for another five years under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), citing its alleged involvement in activities prejudicial to the country's security, communal harmony and secular fabric. ANI | Updated: 13-11-2026 13:43 IST | Created: 13-11-2026 13:43 IST

Fugitive preacher and IRF head Zakri Naik (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

Country:

India

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) on Friday extended the ban on the Islamic Research Foundation (IRF), led by fugitive preacher Dr Zakir Naik, declaring the organisation an unlawful association for another five years under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), citing its alleged involvement in activities prejudicial to the country's security, communal harmony and secular fabric. In a post on X, the Office of the Home Minister Amit Shah said,"In steadfast adherence to PM Shri @narendramodi ji's vision of zero tolerance towards terrorism and anti-national activities, MHA extends the ban on the Islamic Research Foundation as an unlawful association under the UAPA. Led by fugitive terror preacher Dr Zakir Naik, the organisation has been involved in sinister anti-India designs, including inciting communal hatred and promoting terrorism. The group has been found to be propagating a venomous ideology of terrorism and separatism, instigating violent unrest, encouraging the regrouping of absconding terrorists and fomenting communal discord." According to a notification issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the IRF had been indulging in activities prejudicial to the security of the country, with the potential to disturb peace and communal harmony and disrupt the secular fabric of the country. The notification stated that the Central Government had earlier declared the IRF an unlawful association under Section 3(1) of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, through notifications dated November 17, 2016, and November 15, 2021. The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Tribunal, constituted under Section 5 of the Act to adjudicate whether sufficient grounds existed for declaring the organisation unlawful, had subsequently confirmed the declarations through orders published on May 22, 2017, and March 30, 2022. The notification further noted that the existing ban under Section 6(1) of the Act was due to cease on November 14, 2026. The Central Government stated that the IRF and its members, particularly its founder and president, Dr Zakir Abdul Karim Naik alias Dr Zakir Naik, had been encouraging and aiding followers to promote or attempt to promote, on religious grounds, disharmony and feelings of enmity, hatred or ill-will between different religious communities and groups, in a manner prejudicial to the country's integrity and security. The government cited several grounds for its decision, including statements and speeches made by Naik, which it described as "objectionable and subversive". It further alleged that through these speeches and statements, Naik had been promoting enmity and hatred among different religious groups and inspiring youths belonging to a particular religion in India and abroad to commit terrorist acts. The notification also stated that Naik had made radical statements and speeches to millions of people worldwide through international satellite television networks, the internet, print and social media. The Central Government expressed apprehension that if the unlawful activities of the IRF were not curbed and controlled immediately, the organisation could continue its subversive activities and reorganise activists who were still absconding. It further stated that the organisation could disrupt the secular fabric of the country by creating communal disharmony, propagate anti-national sentiments, escalate secessionism by supporting militancy and undertake activities prejudicial to the sovereignty, integrity and security of the country. Invoking Sections 3(1) and 3(3) of the UAPA, 1967, the Central Government declared the Islamic Research Foundation an unlawful association with immediate effect. The notification stated that the declaration would remain in force for a period of five years from the date of its publication in the Official Gazette, subject to any order that may be passed under Section 4 of the Act. (ANI)

item.content:encoded:
IRGC says destruction of US radar in Bahrain was warning to Washington, threatens harsher response to further violations "The destruction of a US radar in Bahrain was a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to end its aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz. If the enemy repeats its violations and acts of aggression, the IRGC Aerospace Force is on full alert to respond without limits," the IRGC said, as reported by Fars News Agency. ANI | Updated: 13-11-2026 12:29 IST | Created: 13-11-2026 12:29 IST

Representative Image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

Country:

Iran

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has claimed that its Aerospace Force destroyed a US early warning radar installation in Bahrain, describing the strike as a serious warning to Washington and threatening a harsher response if the United States repeats what Tehran calls acts of aggression and violations. According to Fars News Agency, the IRGC said the radar was targeted and destroyed in retaliation for an alleged US aerial attack on a telecommunications tower in Iran's Sirik region. The force claimed that its personnel carried out the strike on the US military's early warning radar on Bahrain Island approximately an hour after the attack. In a statement, the IRGC said the destruction of the radar was intended to warn the United States against continuing its aerial operations and what it described as oil smuggling in the strategically important Strait of Hormuz. "The destruction of a US radar in Bahrain was a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to end its aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz. If the enemy repeats its violations and acts of aggression, the IRGC Aerospace Force is on full alert to respond without limits," the IRGC said, as reported by Fars News Agency. The force further warned companies against falling for what it called the enemy's deception, saying those that did so would face harsher penalties. The latest warning comes amid escalating tensions between Iran, the United States and Israel, with the Strait of Hormuz emerging as a key flashpoint in the confrontation. The narrow waterway is a major route for global oil shipments, making security in the region a significant international concern. Earlier, Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei warned countries against providing military or logistical assistance to Washington for its operations against Tehran, saying any direct or indirect involvement would be considered participation in aggression against Iran. In a post on X, Baqaei invoked the United Nations Charter and international law while cautioning governments against supporting US military operations. “A sparrow that tries to fly after a stork will eventually break its legs (Korean proverb),” he said, warning countries against aligning themselves with Washington's military actions. Baqaei said, “Any direct or indirect involvement in acts of aggression or in inhumane economic terrorism against Iran - including the deployment of naval forces, military and logistical support equipment, and personnel - will be regarded as a hostile and unlawful act amounting to participation in the US aggression against Iran. Such actions not only violate Article 2 (4) of the Charter of the United Nations but also fall within the definition of an act of aggression set out in UN General Assembly Resolution 3314.” Rejecting possible justifications for such assistance, he said, “Invoking seemingly legitimate pretexts such as ‘protecting freedom of navigation’ or ‘countering piracy’ does not alter the unlawful and hostile nature of such actions.” “Our message is unequivocal: No bilateral agreement or commitment with the United States can constitute legitimate grounds for violating a state's obligations under international law or for participating in the US-Israeli military aggression against Iran,” Baqaei added. He further warned that any state participating in such actions would bear full responsibility for the consequences. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump, in an interview with Salem News Channel on Thursday (local time), issued a warning to Tehran over any potential threat to American officials. “They will not exist any longer,” Trump said when asked about the possibility of Iran killing US officials, adding that he would have “no hesitation” in using military force. Trump also claimed that the United States had total control over the Strait of Hormuz and said that the Iranian regime was collapsing. (ANI)

item.title: WRAPUP 2-US labor market resilient; existing home sales hit more than 16-year low in October
item.description: Read more about WRAPUP 2-US labor market resilient; existing home sales hit more than 16-year low in October on Devdiscourse ...
item.content:encoded:
WRAPUP 2-US labor market resilient; existing home sales hit more than 16-year low in October Reuters | Updated: 12-11-2026 23:19 IST | Created: 12-11-2026 23:19 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits increased more than expected last week, but remained at a level consistent with a stable labor market, allowing the Federal Reserve to focus on fighting inflation. Economists expect layoffs to remain low through the end of the year, though seasonal volatility related to the holiday season could cause some spikes in the claims data. The government last week reported a surge in nonfarm payrolls in October and a decline in the unemployment rate to 4.1% from 4.2% in September. The resilience in the labor market is despite the ongoing Middle East conflict, which is boosting inflation. "Firms are continuing to hold on to labor," said Olivia Cross, senior US economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics. "We expect layoffs to remain low through the fourth quarter, but then come under some pressure next year in response to the recent tightening of financial conditions and the growing use of AI by firms." Initial claims for state unemployment benefits rose 9,000 to a seasonally adjusted 200,000 for the week ended November 7, the Labor Department said on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 195,000 claims for the latest week. Claims have stayed at or below 200,000 since mid-September and remain close to the 189,000 level touched in mid-July, the lowest since 1969, raising the prospect that the labor market could be tightening. But with wages growing at a moderate pace, most economists do not believe that is the case. Some argue that a smaller workforce, due to retirements and the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, is the key driver of the historically low level of claims. "A generally smaller labor force could mean fewer workers to file for unemployment insurance," said Veronica Clark, an economist at Citigroup. "Of course, this would still be consistent with a low unemployment rate, with continuing claims suggesting the unemployment rate may even fall further towards around 4.0% in data by early 2027." The claims report showed that the number of people receiving unemployment benefits after an initial week of aid, a proxy for hiring, fell 20,000 to a seasonally adjusted 1.697 million during the week ended October 31. But the so-called continuing claims do not include some unemployed people, such as recent college graduates and others who have little or no work history. Some people might also have exhausted their eligibility for benefits, limited to 26 weeks in most states, keeping continuing claims at relatively low levels. The median duration of unemployment jumped to 11.9 weeks in October, the longest since November 2021, from 11.5 weeks in September. Though businesses have been hoarding workers, they have remained reluctant to increase headcount, with economists citing uncertainty from the US-Israeli war with Iran, now in its ninth month. Businesses were also unsure of their staffing needs as they embraced AI. US central bank Governor Michael Barr warned on Thursday the nation should be prepared for "serious short-term disruptions" to the job market because of AI, which he said, depending on how fast it is deployed, could begin displacing workers at scale and widening inequality in favor of investors. Stocks on Wall Street were trading lower as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's exit and rising oil prices following comments by President Donald Trump that the US did not need a deal with Iran weighed on sentiment. The dollar advanced against a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields rose. HOUSE PRICES STILL ELEVATED Government data this week showed consumer prices increasing faster than expected in October. That, together with comments from Fed Governor Christopher Waller, prompted financial markets to almost fully price in a 25-basis-point rate hike in December, and to anticipate another increase in January. The Fed left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range last month. While the labor market continues to hold up, rising mortgage rates stemming from the Iran war are depressing the interest-rate-sensitive housing market. Sales of previously owned homes tumbled 5.5% in October to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million units, the National Association of Realtors said in a separate report. That was the lowest level since August 2010, when sales were declining as a homebuyers tax credit ended. The incentive was aimed at stimulating demand following the 2008 global financial crisis. Economists had forecast home resales falling to a rate of 3.85 million units. Sales plunged 8.8% on a year-over-year basis in October. The drop in sales was across all price categories, including those priced $1 million and above, which had experienced strong growth in prior months. The 30-year fixed mortgage rate jumped above 7% in late August, rising to 7.40% by mid-September, for a total of 142 basis points since the US and Israel attacked Iran at the end of February, data from mortgage finance agency Freddie Mac showed. It averaged 7.11% in the latest week, down from 7.18% in the prior week. "Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023," said Lawrence Yun, the NAR's chief economist. The NAR's Housing Affordability Index dropped to 100.7 from 107.3 in October 2025. Existing housing inventory increased 1.3% to 1.590 million units, the highest level since November 2019. Supply rose 4.6% from a year ago. At October's sales pace, it would take 5.1 months to exhaust the current inventory of existing homes, the most since November 2015. That was up from 4.4 months a year ago. The median existing home price last month advanced 0.4% from a year ago to $421,900, the highest for any October. First-time buyers accounted for 29% of sales, down from 32% a year ago. A 40% share in this category is needed for a robust housing market. The housing market weakness is demand-related, with higher prices keeping distressed sales at a negligible 2%. "With mortgage rates expected to remain above 7% through most of 2027, we expect home sales to remain below 4 million until late next year," said Nancy Vanden Houten, lead US economist at Oxford Economics.
